transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-06
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Ortiz (Redwood SE), Irene Park (Redwood Solutions), Tom B. (Redwood), Priya Nair (CTO, Halcyon), Ethan Ruiz (Eng Mgr), Samira Khan (SRE), Noah Li (Product)

Summary:
Halcyon is evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for a low-latency streaming assistant used in customer-facing flows. Primary goals: p95 latency under 350ms for short-turn prompts (avg 40 tokens), sustained token/sec throughput at 800 tps across bursty traffic with 600 concurrent sessions, and graceful fallback when node pools are saturated. Security and data residency are also concerns. Customer asked for an initial pilot + benchmarks and wanted clarity on routing/fallback policies and KV cache behavior for streaming.

Topics Covered:
- p95 targets and measurement methodology
- Burst vs steady-state throughput and autoscale considerations
- Streaming best practices: chunk sizes, continuous batching, token buffers
- KV cache and prefix caching for chat workloads
- Dedicated sizing and isolation (reserved GPU pools) vs Hosted cost tradeoffs
- Private/VPC options, KMS/HSM, and log retention for SOC2
- Next steps: pilot plan, benchmark run, pricing and SLA discussion

Action items (recap):
- Maya to send pricing and Dedicated sizing spreadsheet
- Luca to provide technical runbook snippets for streaming and caching config
- Priya to share prompt corpus and traffic sample

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro from our side, I'm Maya, AE on the Halcyon account, with Luca and Irene. How's everybody doing?
[00:08] Priya Nair: Doing well, thanks. Excited to get into the latency stuff. We've got a pretty strict p95 target for our conversational webhook flows.
[00:15] Ethan Ruiz: Yeah hi from eng, we mostly care about sustained throughput and how we avoid tail latency spikes during customer bursts.
[00:22] Luca Ortiz: Great, so just to set expectations, we'll walk through typical latency profiles, what impacts p95, and how Redwood handles streaming and fallbacks. If we need to, we can go deep into Dedicated sizing.
[00:33] Samira Khan: Quick note — from SRE side we need audit logs and KMS integration if we do private. SOC2 is non-neg.
[00:40] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll cover security later. First: p95 numbers. Can you share the precise SLA you want?
[00:46] Priya Nair: We're targeting p95 less than 350ms for short prompts, and p95 below 750ms for longer multi-turn responses. Our average prompt size is like 30–50 tokens and responses 50–150 tokens.
[00:58] Luca Ortiz: Okay that helps. Two things drive p95: model compute time (tokens/sec) and serving overhead like batching and queueing. For streaming specifically, prefix caching and KV cache warmness matter a lot — if the chat uses a stable prefix most of the time we can serve the first tokens faster.
[01:12] Noah Li: When you say KV cache, is that automatically enabled in Hosted or only in Dedicated?
[01:16] Luca Ortiz: It's available universally — the runtime supports KV cache and prefix caching across modes. For Hosted we'll handle cache placement for you; on Dedicated you can control eviction windows and pinning policies. There's a tradeoff: more aggressive cache retention reduces cold-starts but costs memory.
[01:29] Ethan Ruiz: Our traffic is spiky — we've got marketing spikes and weekend surges. We're planning for 600 concurrent live sessions at peak, each with streaming tokens coming in at variable rates. Can Redwood sustain 800 token/sec aggregate across the fleet without p95 degradation?
[01:43] Luca Ortiz: The short answer: yes with the right pooling and batching. The longer answer's about batch targets and continuous batching thresholds. For streaming, we try to flush small chunks quickly — so you trade a little throughput for latency. Dedicated gives you more control to tune batch windows; Hosted uses conservative defaults to maintain multi-tenant fairness.
[01:56] Priya Nair: So if we do Dedicated, what's the sizing for 600 concurrent sessions and your target 800 tps?
[02:02] Luca Ortiz: I'll give ballpark numbers — a lot depends on model family and quantization. For a 7B-style model with optimized kernels we usually estimate ~200–250 tokens/sec per GPU for streaming-friendly runs at p95 targets; for 30B it's much lower. That suggests you need ~3–4 GPUs sustained. But to handle bursts and headroom we'd recommend a 6 GPU Dedicated pool with autoscale/burst to handle double peak. We'll put exact curves in the sheet.
[02:24] Ethan Ruiz: Wait, are those per-GPU numbers measured under continuous batching? If we prioritize latency, doesn't batching shrink and metric tokens/sec drop?
[02:31] Luca Ortiz: Correct — if you push batch windows down to 5–10ms to hit 200–300ms p95 for short prompts, your per-GPU throughput drops. That's where smarter routing and kv-prefix help — cache hits are essentially zero compute for early tokens. Also quantized variants can improve tokens/sec with tiny quality regressions.
[02:47] Tom B.: Also want to call out our smart routing — you can configure a low-latency path that routes small interactive requests to a reserved low-batch pool and heavier async jobs to a high-throughput pool. Works cross-region too.
[02:58] Samira Khan: How do fallbacks look? If Dedicated pool saturates, will requests queue or fall back to Hosted? We can't have user-facing errors.
[03:05] Maya Chen: Good question. Redwood supports policy-based fallbacks — can route to a compatible model variant in Hosted or a smaller-generation model in Dedicated. There are also soft-queue approaches that respond with partial streaming tokens and then continue after fallback. We typically recommend an A/B canary for fallback logic and we can auto-failover for config.
[03:23] Priya Nair: Partial tokens sound risky for UX. We need deterministic behavior: either stream smoothly at slightly lower quality or degrade gracefully with a message.
[03:30] Irene Park: Totally — we've seen teams prefer deterministic fallbacks: return a short, slightly higher-latency but complete response rather than chopped streaming pieces. We can help design that in the pilot.
[03:39] Ethan Ruiz: Security again: if we fallback from Private to Hosted, how does data residency and encryption behave?
[03:45] Luca Ortiz: If you require strict data residency, we can restrict fallback policies to only route within allowed regions or not at all. For encryption, KMS/HSM keys remain customer-managed on Private; Hosted fallback would need explicit agreement and data handling terms — we can avoid sensitive payloads from leaving the VPC.
[03:59] Noah Li: Any real-world numbers you can share? I mean like p95 with streaming on your hosted tenants?
[04:05] Luca Ortiz: On our standard hosted config with low-latency pools, for a 7B open family model we've seen p95s around 250–450ms for short 40-token prompts depending on region and network. But full transparency: transcription/perf numbers vary across corpora. We'll run your corpus.
[04:21] Priya Nair: Good — we will provide prompts. Also curious about observability: can we get per-route p95 and token-level breakdowns?
[04:28] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Console has per-route / per-model dashboards, token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and tracing hooks you can emit to Jaeger/Datadog. You can set alerts on regressions.
[04:37] Samira Khan: For the pilot, we need an audit trail of config changes. Is that available in Dedicated?
[04:42] Irene Park: Yes, Dedicated and Private both have audit logs and RBAC. We'll include the retention windows in the security doc.
[04:48] Ethan Ruiz: Let's talk about benchmarking. We want a reproducible benchmark that simulates 600 concurrent sessions, with a mix: 60% short prompts, 30% mid, 10% long. Can Redwood run that or do you want us to run it?
[04:59] Luca Ortiz: We can run it on a Redwood test rig or we can give you an automation script. For fidelity I'd recommend us running the first pass on a mirrored Dedicated pool so we control variables. Then we'll hand you the harness to reproduce. We also want your prompt corpus to include edge cases.
[05:14] Priya Nair: Ok schedule-wise — if we do benchmark next Tues, how long would it take?
[05:19] Luca Ortiz: The benchmark run itself is a couple hours to sweep parameters. Data analysis and an findings deck ~2 business days.
[05:24] Maya Chen: We'll include throughput vs p95 curves and recommended Dedicated sizing and carbon headroom.
[05:29] Noah Li: Anything about quantization? We have some concern about hallucination increases.
[05:33] Luca Ortiz: Quantization can slightly affect quality; we'll include a small eval set to measure regression. Often 4-bit quantization on specific kernels is a good tradeoff for throughput. We'll surface quality numbers per prompt.
[05:43] Ethan Ruiz: On cost — can you give a hosted vs dedicated rough monthly cost for the recommended 6 GPU pool?
[05:49] Maya Chen: I'll send the committed capacity pricing versus pay-as-you-go hosted rates in the sheet. We also model per-token economics for the pilot traffic.
[05:56] Priya Nair: Great. A couple of smaller technical questions: 1) how do you handle KV cache eviction and pinning? 2) What's the default streaming chunk size?
[06:03] Luca Ortiz: Eviction defaults to LRU with a configurable TTL per customer and ability to pin sessions for a short duration. Streaming chunk size defaults to 64 tokens/100ms window depending on model, but can be tuned down to 16 tokens/30ms for ultra-low-latency paths.
[06:17] Samira Khan: And does the client SDK support resuming streams if connection drops?
[06:21] Irene Park: Yes, we have reconnect semantics and sequence tokens so clients can resume from last acked chunk. We'll include sample SDK calls.
[06:29] Priya Nair: Last thing — our compliance team will ask about SOC2, ISO and an incident disclosure SLA. Can you share those docs?
[06:36] Maya Chen: Yep, we'll share security pack and SOC2 report. For incidents we have tiered notifications and postmortem commitments.
[06:43] Ethan Ruiz: Ok let's recap next steps.
[06:45] Maya Chen: Recap: 1) We'll run a pilot benchmark next Tue (Mar 10) on a mirrored Dedicated pool, 2) Maya sends pricing and Dedicated sizing spreadsheet by Mar 8, 3) Luca shares streaming config snippets and example benchmark harness by Mar 9, 4) Priya shares prompt corpus and traffic profile by Mar 8. Any additions?
[06:59] Priya Nair: That covers it. We'll also want a 30-minute follow-up after the benchmark to review findings.
[07:04] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with calendar invites and the sheet.
[07:09] Meeting end.
